summary: Find all unique combinations (each candidate used at most once, candidates may repeat) that sum to the target.
mainInsight: Sort so duplicates are adjacent; recurse with i + 1 (no reuse) and, within the same loop level, skip a candidate equal to the previous one (`i > start and c[i] == c[i-1]`) so identical combinations are not produced twice.

approaches.name: Generate all and de-duplicate with a set
approaches.summary: Collect sorted tuples in a set.

approaches.name: Sort + backtracking with sibling skipping
approaches.summary: Skip equal values at the same recursion level.

personalSolution.notes: Optimal; add a break when candidates[i] > remaining for extra pruning.

promptVariants: How do you avoid duplicate combinations when the input has duplicate values?
What is the standard skip condition?
options: Sort, then skip c[i] when i > start and c[i] == c[i-1]
cards.answer: Sort, then skip c[i] when i > start and c[i] == c[i-1]
cards.explanation: At a given level, trying the same value twice yields identical subtrees.

promptVariants: Why is the condition `i > start` and not `i > 0`?
What is the difference between reusing a duplicate at the same level vs a deeper level?
cards.answer: At the same loop level, choosing the second copy of a value after already trying the first produces the same set of combinations again, so skip it (i > start). At a deeper level (the next recursion, where i == start) the second copy may legitimately be used together with the first, e.g. [1,1,6]. `i > 0` would wrongly forbid that.
keyPoints: Deeper levels may use the next copy
cards.explanation: That is the heart of Subsets II and Permutations II too.

promptVariants: Complete the statement: Worst-case time (n candidates): ___
cards.explanation: Each element is either chosen or not; sorting adds O(n log n).

promptVariants: What is the auxiliary space excluding the output?
How much auxiliary memory does Combination Sum II need besides the result?
cards.answer: O(n) for the recursion depth and the current path.

promptVariants: Why does the loop use `choose(i + 1, ...)` and where could sorting give an early `break`?
cards.answer: i + 1 ensures each element is used at most once. choose(i, ...) would allow reuse (Combination Sum). Because the array is sorted, once candidates[i] > remaining every later one also overshoots, so you can `break` as soon as that happens (instead of recursing and returning).
cards.explanation: Sorting is what makes the skip condition valid.

promptVariants: For candidates [1,1,2], target 3 what are the results?
options: [[1,2]] (the second 1 would repeat the same combination)
cards.answer: [[1,2]] (the second 1 would repeat the same combination)
cards.explanation: Using either 1 gives the same multiset [1,2]; sibling skipping emits it once.

incorrectOptionExplanations.[[1,1,1]]: There are only two 1s in the input, so three cannot be used.
